header.title: Libros quinque adversus haereses: AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Irenaeus, Saint, Bishop of Lyon
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's tlg1447.tlg001.1st1K-grc1, from Open Greek and Latin's First1KGreek (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg1447.tlg001.1st1K-gr: Footnote numerals printed inside the Greek are not translated. 'αὐτὴ l. ἐ. αὐτὴν' carries an editor's correction (read αὐτήν, object of ἐπιστρεψάντων); translated on that reading.

Line 1 joins two texts: a parallel summary ('Another of their teachers ... often taking a cup, etc.'), an editor's cross-reference ('κ.τ.λ. infra not. 3, p. 115', not translated), and then the continuation of Irenaeus's own sentence from the preceding lines, where ἔχοντι ('possessing') completes 'the greatest power from the invisible and unnameable places'. 'Trickery with gifts' (κυβείας δώρων) is odd and may be corrupt. In both lines the Greek carries footnote numerals and variant notes (Int., Hipp., Hippol., l. ...), which are not translated. 'We must become established as one' follows the editor's suggested reading δεῖ ἡμᾶς ἓν καταστῆσαι for the garbled δι᾿ ἡμᾶς ἐγκαταστῆσαι. 'Adorned' renders κεκοσμημένον; the variant κεκομισμένον would mean 'brought'. The article before χαυνωθεῖσα ('And she') is missing in the text; μαὶ, οἷμα, εὐχαρισιεῖν, ἐμῦς, πνείματος read as καὶ, αἷμα, εὐχαριστεῖν, ἐμῆς, πνεύματος.

nodes.text: Another of their teachers, Marcus, skilled in magic, deceived many, partly through trickery with gifts and incantations, partly also through demons. He said that the greatest power from the invisible and unnameable places was in him. And indeed often taking a cup, etc. [...] possessing [it]; so that he has been shown to be truly a forerunner of the Antichrist. For mixing the tricks of Anaxilaus with the knavery of the so-called magi, and producing illusions and working magic by means of them, he threw those who watched him and trusted him into amazement. And those who see the works of his curious arts think that certain powers are being worked by his hands. For they too have lost their minds and do not see, not knowing how to test it, that the contrivance of his trick is accomplished, so to speak, by magic.

2. Pretending to give thanks over cups mixed with wine, and drawing out the words of the invocation at greater length, he makes them appear purple and red, so that it seems that Grace, from the regions above all things, is dripping her own blood into that cup through his invocation, and those present long exceedingly to taste of that drink, so that the Grace called down by this magician may rain on them too. Again, handing mixed cups to women, he bids them give thanks over them while he stands by. And when this has been done, he himself brings forward another cup much larger than the one over which the deluded woman gave thanks, and pours from the smaller one, over which the woman gave thanks, into the one adorned by him, saying at the same time these words: "May the Grace that is before all things, unthinkable and ineffable, fill your inner man and multiply her knowledge in you, sowing the grain of mustard seed in the good earth." And saying some such things, and driving the wretched woman into a frenzy, he appeared a wonder-worker, when the large cup was filled from the small one, so that it even overflowed. And by doing certain other things like these he has deceived many and drawn them away after him. It is likely that he also has some demon as his *paredros* [attendant spirit], through whom he himself seems to prophesy, and through whom he makes to prophesy as many women as he thinks worthy to share in his grace. For he busies himself above all with women, and of these with those who wear fine-bordered and purple-edged robes and are richest; and often, trying to lead them on, he says to them, flattering: "I want to give you a share of my Grace, since the Father of all sees your angel continually before his face. The place of the Greatness is in us; we must become established as one. Receive grace first from me and through me. Prepare yourself as a bride awaiting her bridegroom, so that you may be what I am, and I what you are. Establish the seed of light in your bridal chamber. Receive the bridegroom from me, and make room for him, and be held in him. Behold, grace has come down upon you; open your mouth and prophesy." When the woman answers, "I have never prophesied, and I do not know how to prophesy," he makes certain invocations a second time, to astound the woman he is deceiving, and says to her: "Open your mouth, say anything at all, and you will prophesy." And she, puffed up and made a fool of by what has been said, her soul heated by the expectation that she is about to prophesy, her heart beating more than it should, ventures to speak, and speaks nonsense and whatever comes, all of it emptily and boldly, as one heated by an empty spirit (as one better than us said of such people, that a soul heated by empty air is a bold and shameless thing); and from then on she takes herself for a prophetess, and thanks Marcus for giving her a share of his own grace; and she tries to repay him, not only by the gift of her possessions (which is how he has amassed a great quantity of money) but also by the sharing of her body, eager to be united with him in everything, so that she may go down with him into the One.

4. That this Marcus also instils love-potions and *agōgima* [spells to draw a lover] in some of the women, though not in all, so as to outrage their very bodies, these women, often after returning to the church of God, have confessed: both that they had been defiled in body by him and that they had loved him with great passion. So that a certain deacon too, one of our people in Asia, who had received him into his house, fell into this calamity: his wife, who was beautiful, was corrupted in both mind and body by this magician and followed him for a long time; afterwards, when the brethren had with much toil converted her, she spent all her time in confession, mourning and lamenting over the corruption she had suffered from the magician.
